# DeepWork — full page

> Source: https://deepwork.rajatmalik.dev/

> rendered page. A shorter, curated index is at /llms.txt.

Free · MIT licensed · v3.0.0

## Focus better. Work deeper.

DeepWork is a free focus timer, task list, day planner and habit tracker in one window — and it keeps every byte on your own machine. Now it also remembers what the hours were for, and keeps asking about the one thing you cannot afford to miss. No account. No cloud. No subscription.

New in 3.0 — Time by Task, standing reminders and quiet controls →
- Windows · macOS · Linux · any browser
- Offline AI · no cloud
- Works offline

The product

### One window for the whole working day

DeepWork is not a timer with a task list bolted on. It is a single window where the session you are running, the work you promised yourself, the day you planned and the progress you made all live in the same place.

#### The focus clock

Work, short break and long break on one ring that fills as the session runs.

#### One board, three columns

Drag a card between To Do, In Progress and Done — its colour is its status.

#### Keyboard first

Focused cards move along the board with 1, 2, 3 and the arrow keys. Ctrl+N adds a task.

#### Everything on one page

Today, Matrix, Calendar, Habits, Journal and Insights are one click apart.

New in 3.0

### What changed since you last looked

This page described version 2.0.17. Since then the app gained a new page, a new kind of reminder and a quieter set of controls — plus a long list of smaller corrections. These are the ones that change how a working day actually goes.
- New pageTime by TaskEvery focus session grouped by the work it paid for. A daily Code review becomes one line with one total, one rhythm and one consistency figure — not thirty rows to add up.Read the section →

#### Time by Task

Every focus session grouped by the work it paid for. A daily Code review becomes one line with one total, one rhythm and one consistency figure — not thirty rows to add up.
- New featureStanding RemindersA reminder for the presentation, the class or the dose that keeps asking — on the desktop, in the app, and after a restart — until you press Done, Snooze or Stop.Read the section →

A reminder for the presentation, the class or the dose that keeps asking — on the desktop, in the app, and after a restart — until you press Done, Snooze or Stop.
- New controlsA pause that pauses everythingPause, mute and focus in one panel on every surface, a mute that ends by itself, and a completion alert that can be answered without opening the window.Read the section →

#### A pause that pauses everything

Pause, mute and focus in one panel on every surface, a mute that ends by itself, and a completion alert that can be answered without opening the window.

Also new

#### Release by release

Shipped between 2.0.18 and 3.0.0, in the app’s own words. The three headlines above have their own sections; this is everything else.
- 3.0

##### A tray menu for the work

New task opens quick-add from wherever the app is, Settings brings the full window up on the right page, Pause offers 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes, and the mute moved into a submenu of its own lengths.
- 3.0

##### A first launch that asks once

One dialog offers to start DeepWork with the computer. Not now is an answer: it starts four or five quiet nudges a day, each with a Stop asking button, instead of asking the same question every launch.
- 3.0

##### A taskbar reminder that tells the truth

Windows will not let an ordinary app pin itself. DeepWork asks the shell first; where the request would be refused, the button becomes Yes, show me and opens the app list where you can pin it.
- 3.0

##### A matrix that gives its space back

A folded quadrant becomes a one-line strip and the open quadrants reflow into the room. The dividers drag by mouse or arrow keys, and the split is remembered as a share of the board.
- 3.0

##### Settings that fill the screen

Settings and About now pack as many 380–600 px cards as the window fits, with the reading measure kept inside each card, instead of a 560 px strip in the middle of a 1920 px monitor.
- 3.0

##### An app that knows how it is running

The desktop app, an installed web app and a browser tab are three different surfaces. The install dialog explains the one route this browser actually has, and an installed web app is told what it cannot do.
- 3.0

##### Every question answerable where it is asked

The startup, taskbar and water questions carry Yes and Not now on their desktop notification, and the completion alert carries Pause, Next, Resume and Hold up — so answering does not mean finding the window.
- 2.0.22

##### A timeline that says what is running

The session in progress is drawn inside the span it was booked for, and its own start and end times sit on the card instead of in a hover tooltip.
- 2.0.22

##### Today stays today

Add to Today now carries the day it was set on. Yesterday’s starred work no longer follows you into this morning’s board, and a session started without a task is no longer filed against last week’s task.
- 2.0.21

##### The database is protected like the only copy it is

The file is checked read-only before it is opened; a database that is there and unreadable stops startup instead of being replaced by an empty one; and every launch copies it into a backups folder before migrations touch it.
- 2.0.20

##### Edit a task where you read it

A pencil on every board and matrix card, an edit control in the calendar, and Edit task on the dashboard’s current-focus card all open the one task form with the task already in its fields.
- 2.0.20

##### Add to the day you are looking at

Today carries Add task, each date section has its own +, and every matrix quadrant has one that opens the form already in that quadrant.
- 2.0.20

##### An update you can turn down for good

The update card gained Skip this version — that release is never offered again — while closing it and Remind me later are a twelve-hour snooze, not a silent goodbye.
- 2.0.19

##### Always on top now stays on top

The flag is written straight to the window and read back from it, and a watcher re-asserts it when another application, a display change or a fullscreen window takes the spot away.
- 2.0.18

##### A drink is 30 ml, and the reminder is on

The water nudge is on by default and counts the smallest thing anyone would call a drink, so a day of sipping adds up honestly instead of a handful of guesses at half a litre each.
- 2.0.18

##### A visitor count, said out loud

The hosted web app counts visits with GoatCounter. It is off with one switch, never runs in the desktop build, and sends the page — never a task, a journal entry or an identifier.

More than a Pomodoro

### A timer counts down. DeepWork keeps the whole day.

Most focus timers stop at the countdown and hand the rest of your day back to a note app and a spreadsheet. DeepWork keeps going: what you are working on, when you planned to do it, whether you did it, how you slept on it, and what the pattern looks like after a month.
- Focus sessions The Pomodoro timer
- Day planner A timeline that schedules your tasks
- Tasks Board, dates and deadlines
- Eisenhower matrix Four quadrants, drag to prioritise
- Today Only the work that belongs to today
- Time by Task The work your hours actually went to
- Standing reminders They keep asking until you answer
- Habits Check in, keep a streak
- Journal A dated entry per day
- Water reminder Asks, counts, and stays quiet outside your hours
- Insights Offline AI reads your own numbers
- Import & export Excel and CSV in, CSV and JSON out
- Quiet controls Pause, mute and focus on every surface
- Desktop behaviour Tray, mini widget, always on top
- Local database One SQLite file, on your machine

All of it in one local app, with no account and nothing uploaded.

Focus sessions

### A session you can actually finish

Start the clock, and the rest of the app gets quiet. One ring fills as the session runs, in the window and in the mini widget, so however you are working you are looking at the same countdown.
- Focus session 25 min
- Short break 5 min
- Long break 15 min
- Four sessions, then a long break The cycle you would expect from Pomodoro, and every part of it is a setting: the three lengths and how many sessions come before the long one.
- An alert that will not be missed A finished session rings, raises a system notification, and moves both the widget and the card to the next of twelve colours — repeating until you answer it. Start, skip or stop answers it too.
- An alert you can answer The completion alert carries Pause, Next, Resume and Hold up. Next moves on and starts the next session, and a crossed alert comes back after three minutes — because swiping it away is not an answer.
- Tones generated, not downloaded Four choices — bell, chime, ding or none — synthesised with the Web Audio API, with the volume under your system controls and a tray mute.
- A sentence, not a beep Every finished session draws a different line from twenty-four written for focus and twenty-four for breaks, walked in order so the same one does not come back twice.

> “That was a session, not a sprint. Step away while it settles.” One of the twenty-four focus lines the app ends a session with.

Day planner

### Plan the day in focus blocks, not in hope

Most planners ask you to guess how long something takes. DeepWork already knows the size of a focus block, so it lays your day out for you — and then gets out of the way when you want to move something yourself.

The totals the Calendar keeps for a day — counted from the timeline itself.

#### It does the arithmetic

Your queued tasks become focus blocks on a real timeline, with breaks already reserved between them. You see the day you have, not the day you hoped for.

#### Priority decides the order

Work is queued by Eisenhower quadrant, then by the order you put it in. The first thing on the timeline is the thing you said mattered.

#### Pin it, and the plan bends

Drag a task onto a time and it stays there. A task can span several blocks, and a block can hold more than one task if you put them there yourself.

#### Fit day

When the queue does not fit the window, one button extends the day until everything has a place — or tells you honestly that it still does not.

#### A day that ends

The day window is yours to set. Outside it, DeepWork is not pretending you are working.

#### Totals for the day

Focus minutes, break minutes, pomodoros, breaks and tasks — the shape of the day, before you have to remember it.

Tasks

### A board that keeps up with the day

Three columns, and a card moves between them by being dragged or by a single key. What makes it useful is what happens around that: the date filing, the keyboard, and the fact that your existing spreadsheet is not thrown away.
- Cards are dragged between columns — the colour is the status, everywhere at once.
- On Tasks the board is filed by date and the sections fold away, so a long list stays readable.
- Today shows only today: an overdue task, one dated today, or one written today and starred onto it.
- The star that puts a task on Today carries the day it was set on, so yesterday’s starred work expires instead of following you in.
- Unfinished work carries forward by default. Turn it off and yesterday closes itself.
- A pencil on every card — board, matrix, calendar, dashboard — opens the one task form with the task already in its fields.
- Every date section has its own +, Today has Add task, and each matrix quadrant has one that opens the form in that quadrant.

#### Adding a task takes one field

The round add button floats on every page and Ctrl+N opens the same dialog. Type a title and press Add to Today — priority, deadline, quadrant and repeat are already decided, and Advanced options is there if you disagree.

#### Work that comes back

A task can repeat daily, weekly or monthly, on the weekdays you choose, with an end date. Recurring work arrives as its own instance, so finishing today’s does not erase next week’s.

#### Your spreadsheet still works

Import.xlsx,.xlsm or.csv — with a downloadable template that documents every column — and see a validated preview before a single row is written. Repeated titles are labelled, never silently dropped.

#### An export that opens cleanly

Twenty-four columns per task, quick ranges from today to all time, filters by status and priority, and an optional totals block. Written as UTF-8 with a BOM so Excel shows your accents and em dashes correctly.

Prioritisation

### Decide once, in four boxes

A long task list is not a plan. The matrix is where a task stops being a line and becomes a decision — and the decision is what the rest of the app works from. Fold a quadrant and the board gives its space to the ones still open.
- Drag a card into a quadrant and its priority stops being a feeling.
- The task list beside the board is resizable, and every quadrant scrolls on its own.
- Collapse a quadrant, or the whole list, and the board still accepts a drop.
- Quadrant order is what the day planner schedules from — Q1 first, Q4 last.
- Insights shows completion per quadrant, so you can see where your work actually sits.

Schedule folded into a strip. The three open quadrants took the space it gave up.

#### The space comes back

A collapsed quadrant used to hide its contents and keep its share of the board, which is why minimising Schedule never made Do First any bigger. Now the board reflows around what is open, and the split is yours to drag.
- Three open quadrants put the first across the top and the other two side by side underneath; two sit side by side; one takes the whole board.
- Maximise is the same thing as collapsing the other three, so there is one rule to understand rather than two.
- Restore the layout hands back exactly what was there before.
- The dividers drag by mouse or by arrow keys, with Home and End to even them out; neither side can go below 15%.
- The split is stored as a share of the board, not as pixels, so it survives a window resize and comes back when a quadrant is reopened.

Time by Task

### The work your hours actually went to

Your Code review is a new task row every morning. Count the rows and you learn nothing. Time by Task groups every focus session by the work’s title, so a daily routine becomes one line — one total, one first session, one last, one rhythm.
- It groups the work, not the row Code review on Monday and Code review on Tuesday become one line: one all-time total, one first session, one last, one rhythm.
- It answers over months Active days, sessions, average block and consistency sit beside the total, so a habit and a project do not look the same.
- The shape has names Repeats daily, weekly or monthly, multi-day, one-off or untasked — the rhythm is detected from the days worked, and a configured recurrence wins when there is one.
- The sessions are still there Open a row for the breakdown by week, the averages and the individual sessions behind the number.
- Untasked time is shown Time the timer recorded without a task appears as Untasked focus, with the one sentence that fixes it next time, instead of being quietly dropped.

> “Read the shape, not only the total.” The heading on the page’s own reading card.

This month, grouped by work. The reading above the list is written from the same rows.

The range switch
- Today the hours since midnight
- This week since Monday
- This month the default view
- This year month by month
- All time everything recorded
- Custom any two dates, or one day twice

What a bar means
- Repeating work daily, weekly or monthly
- One-off a single piece of work
- Multi-day one task across several days
- Untasked time recorded without a task

One solid colour per bar. The ring around a bar is “now” — this day, week, month or year — not a second colour to decode.

#### Open the row. The total becomes evidence.

A single figure can be a coincidence. The detail sheet is what lets you check it — and what lets the list stay a list, because the row itself keeps a fixed height.
- This period and all time, side by side.
- Average session length, and consistency across the days in the span.
- A week-by-week table of time, sessions and days.
- The recent sessions themselves, with their start times and durations.

The list is virtualised: only the rows inside the scroll viewport exist in the page, so a year of work scrolls like a page rather than building a thousand cards.

Habits & journal

### The part that is not about the timer at all

Focus sessions measure output. Habits and a journal measure whether the way you work is actually working — and both live in the same app, counted the same way, on the same dates.

Habits

#### Streaks that show their working

- Add a habit with a name and an icon — nothing else is asked for.
- Check in with one press; the streak, the best run and the all-time count follow you.
- A 30-day strip shows exactly which days you missed, not just the percentage.
- A habit below 40% is marked as slipping, in the app’s own words.
- Insights turns the same check-ins into a 30-day consistency chart.

Journal

#### One page a day, and the numbers it leaves

- One entry per day, dated, saved as you type — with Ctrl+S when you want to be sure.
- Writing prompts if the blank page is the problem.
- Days written, words all-time, average entry and the current and best streak.
- Journal-wide consistency for the last 30 days.
- The one comparison worth making: how your focus differs on the days you wrote.

> What went well today? What could be improved? What are you grateful for? A prompt the journal offers when the page is empty.

Hydration

### Stay focused without forgetting the basics

Deep work is not the only thing a long afternoon is missing. The water reminder is on out of the box — it asks a question rather than announcing a fact, so “Not now” is one click — and a drink counts as 30 ml, the smallest thing anyone would call a drink.

#### Every answer is a choice, not a field

The useful range for each setting is narrow, and a number you have to type is a number you can mistype. So the reminder offers the sensible ones and nothing else.
- Remind me every 15 · 20 · 25 · 30 · 45 · 60 · 90 · 120 · 180 min default 60
- One drink counts as 30 · 50 · 70 · 90 · 100 · 150 · 200 · 250 · 300 · 400 · 500 · 750 · 1000 ml default 30 ml
- Daily target 1.5 · 2 · 2.5 · 3 L default 2 L
- Working hours A from and a to time — reminders fire between them default 09:00 – 18:00

#### Today, on the dashboard

The card reads out the day against the target, how many drinks that is, when the last one was and what the reminder is doing next. + 250 ml logs a glass at the size you chose; Undo takes it back if you pressed it twice.

> “Focus is easier when you are not quietly dehydrated.” One of the ten lines the water reminder rotates through.

Each drink is a row of its own, so the day’s total is a sum rather than a counter that can only go up — and the tally starts again at local midnight, not at UTC midnight.

The water card, as it sits on the dashboard.

#### It asks, it does not announce

A card appears with the glass, the day so far and two answers: “Yes, I drank …” logs it, “Not now” closes it. Nothing else dismisses it — not a timer, not a click elsewhere — so a reminder cannot be lost by standing up for a minute.

#### It is on out of the box

The nudge is on by default and counts 30 ml a drink — the smallest thing anyone would call a drink — so a day of sipping adds up honestly. Both are still choices in Settings.

#### It can be answered on the notification

When the reminder arrives as a desktop notification, Yes, drank logs the glass and Not now closes it. Either answer takes the notification down again.

#### It never stacks

An unanswered question holds the cadence, and the next one starts counting from your answer. “Yes” at 14:00 means the next is a full interval later, not one that was already overdue.

#### Quiet when it should be

Outside your working hours it says nothing, and the dashboard tells you when it resumes. A machine that only slept gets one reminder when it wakes, never a queue of the ones it slept through.

#### Minimised means busy

Shrinking DeepWork into the mini widget is you saying you are working elsewhere. The reminder rings, counts the glass and leaves your window alone — unless you turn that off.

#### The clock only runs while the app does

Closing DeepWork pauses the cadence instead of the wall clock charging you for it, so reopening waits a full interval rather than asking the moment the window appears.

#### Undo, because you will double-tap

Each drink is a row of its own, so today’s total is a sum rather than a counter that only goes up — and the last one can be taken back.

A habit nudge, not medical advice — as the app itself puts it. Anyone with a reason to drink more or less water is the person who knows their own number.

Insights

### Understand how you work, not just how long

Every figure on this page is computed on your own machine from your own sessions, tasks, habits and entries. Nothing is uploaded. An offline AI reads those rows, turns them into plain-language analysis, and shows you where you are on track and what to aim for next.

#### What the numbers say

Charts are easy to look at and hard to read. So every chart is paired with a sentence about it, and the sentences are the point:
- You have focused 5 days in a row — the habit is doing the work.
- Best habit: Reading at 82% over 30 days (11-day streak).
- Focus is longest between 09:00 and 11:00 — 34% of all your focus.
- Focus averages 96m on the days you wrote, against 61m on the days you did not.

Examples of the readings DeepWork writes — offline AI analysis of your own rows, computed on your machine and never in the cloud.
- Key figures with a trend Focus time, sessions and tasks, each with its change and a sparkline
- What the numbers say Plain-language readings written from your own data
- Focus consistency A 12-week heatmap — one square per day, darker for more focus
- When you focus Focus by hour of day, with your peak window called out
- Average focus by weekday Where the week actually goes
- Task flow Created against closed, week by week, for 8 weeks
- Where your work sits Completion by Eisenhower quadrant
- Habit consistency 30 days of check-ins with completion rate, current and best streak
- Journalling Days written, words, average entry, and how focus differs on days you wrote
- Recent sessions Average session length and the share of sessions you interrupted

Standing reminders

### A reminder that does not give up

Write down the one thing you cannot afford to forget. When its moment arrives it keeps asking — on the desktop, in the app, and after a restart — until you answer it. It never brings the window forward, and a closed laptop is not an answer.

Two standing, one kept. The card in front is the question; the count behind it is the queue.
- It escalates, not repeats A quick first nudge, then longer gaps — three, five, ten, fifteen, twenty minutes, then every thirty for Insistent. The gap is measured from the last actual ring, so a snooze cannot shorten it.
- It is stored, not scheduled A closed laptop is not an answer. Open the app after lunch and the morning’s reminder is still waiting, with the time it was due and the line “We kept it for you.”
- One at a time Two things due together are a queue, not a stack of cards to dismiss. The card says how many are waiting behind it, and answering the first brings the next forward.
- Crossing is not answering A notification swiped away in the middle of a call comes back after three minutes — because you were busy, not because you meant no.
- It never steals the stage No window jumps in front of the room. The question waits on the sticky desktop notification and in the app, which is exactly where it can be answered without interrupting the presentation it is about.
- Three exits, no cross Done keeps the promise. Snooze 10 min moves it on. Stop ends it honestly. Done and Stop are kept apart in the history, because one is an achievement and the other is a decision.

Three rhythms

#### Pick how hard it insists

The rhythm is the user’s choice at the moment of writing it down — not a technical setting. Every ladder ends in the same last gap repeating, because none of them ever gives up.
- Insistent 3 · 5 · 10 · 15 · 20 · then every 30 min A presentation, a class, a dose or a train.
- Steady 10 · 20 · 30 · 45 · 60 · then every 60 min An ordinary appointment.
- Gentle 30 · 45 · 60 · 90 · 120 · then every 120 min Something that can wait.

The card, at its own size. There is no cross in the corner and no timeout; the only exits are the three buttons.

#### It is not a calendar event, and not a task

A standing reminder has no quadrant, no project and no completion semantics beyond “handled”, because the things it exists for — a presentation, a class, a dose, a train — are often not work at all.
- Done, Snooze 10 min, Stop. The same three answers travel on the desktop notification.
- A pause holds it; the mute does not. A pause stops the asking without erasing the reminder, and the overdue one speaks when the pause ends.
- No quiet-hours bypass. A reminder respects the pause you set and the quiet hours your OS decides on; it does not override either.

Your data

### It stays on your machine, and that is the feature

Most productivity apps ask you to hand over your working life before they will show you a timer. DeepWork asks for nothing: no account, no cloud, no analytics on your work. The hosted web app counts visits and this page counts its own, both are described here, and the app’s can be switched off.
- One SQLite file, copied before it is touched Tasks, sessions, habits, journal entries, water and settings live in a local database. Every launch copies it and its write-ahead log into a backups folder before migrations run, and a database that is there but unreadable stops startup with its path instead of being replaced by an empty one.
- No account, ever Nothing to sign up for, nothing to sign in to, and no email address collected — there is no mechanism to collect one.
- A short list of calls you can name The update check reads the public GitHub release list for the app you are running. An installer is downloaded only when you press Update. Links open in your own browser. That is the complete list for the desktop app — and the hosted web app has one more, below.
- A real exit One JSON file exports sessions, tasks, habits, journal and water records, and importing it restores them after a confirmation. The task list also exports to a 24-column CSV you can open in Excel — not a format only this app reads.

The same app, the same data, in the light theme. Both themes are designed rather than inverted.

The visit count

#### The web app and this page count visits

The app has no server of its own, so the web build uses GoatCounter — the same counter that runs on the author’s site. It exists so “is anybody using this?” has an answer without DeepWork running a backend.
- It is GoatCounter, on the hosted web app — never the desktop build.
- It sends the page — path, title, referrer, screen width, language and time zone — never a task, a journal entry or an identifier.
- GoatCounter stores no IP address and sets no cookie of its own for this.
- Count my visits is a switch in Settings → Visitor Counter → Details. With it off the script is never fetched at all.
- The desktop build is never counted: it has no web address to report, and its Settings row says so.

This page counts its own visits the same way, on its own GoatCounter site, deepwork.goatcounter.com, so the two never mix in a dashboard. It sends the address, the title, the referring site and the screen width; it sets no cookie, GoatCounter stores no IP address, and no third-party script is loaded to make the request — the page sends the beacon itself. A browser that asks not to be tracked is not counted, and the Site stats button in the footer only asks GoatCounter for the totals back.

Backups

#### The database is the only copy

The one piece of state that exists nowhere else gets treated that way: checked before it is opened, copied before it is migrated, and never quietly replaced by an empty file that looks the same.
- The file is checked read-only before anything opens it, so the check cannot itself be the thing that loses the data.
- A truncated file, or one whose committed changes are still in its write-ahead log, is treated as data to protect rather than as an empty file to replace.
- Backups are kept rather than rotated: a rolling series is the only thing that helps after a bad upgrade.
- Every migration this app has shipped adds to the schema; none drops a table, a column or a row.

#### Five log files you can actually open

When something goes wrong on a machine nobody can sit in front of, the app has already written down what it was doing. Settings has one button that opens the folder and another that copies the last 300 lines with the environment they happened in.
- deepwork.log — everything, in order
- system.log — app, window, tray and OS events
- flow.log — pages, timer, imports and exports
- crash.log — panics, unhandled errors and app crashes
- network.log — failed requests, going offline and back

Each file rolls over at 512 KB, keeps its five most recent archives, and can never grow past roughly 15 MB. Identical lines inside two seconds are folded into one with a count, so a repeating fault cannot flood the file.

#### Offline is the normal case

The fonts travel with the app, the alert tones are synthesised rather than downloaded, and the database is a file on your disk. Nothing in the app needs the network to look like itself or to keep your records.
- Inter and JetBrains Mono ship with the build — no font CDN, no third-party request.
- The browser build registers a service worker, so it keeps working after the first visit.
- Dark, light, or follow the system — applied before the first paint, with no flash of the wrong one.

Desktop

### An app, not a tab you will close

The desktop build is the same DeepWork you already know, with the parts a browser cannot give you: a tray icon, an always-on-top timer and a floating widget. That is the honest reason to install it.

A full dialog on first launch offers to start DeepWork when you sign in, leading with what that is worth. No installer writes a startup entry — you ask for it, in the app — and an install whose entry already exists never sees the question.

Keeps the window above everything else, so the timer stays visible while you work in another application. The flag is read back from the window and re-asserted when another application, a display change or a fullscreen window takes the spot away.

The window’s close button puts DeepWork next to the clock instead of ending it, so a session can finish and ring while the window is hidden. Exit in the tray menu is how you really quit.

The mini widget

#### Minimise it and it keeps working

- A 136×76 floating widget with genuinely transparent, rounded corners — the desktop shows through them.
- Draggable anywhere, always above other windows, with play, skip and stop that work without expanding it.
- The same countdown ring as the full window, filling in the same direction at the same speed.
- When a session ends it becomes a bell: one press answers the alert and leaves the timer where it was.
- On a repeat it shakes — for a length you choose, from 0.7 s to 4 s — and moves to the next of twelve colours.
- Esc, or the arrow, restores the full window at its original size, fitted to the screen it lands on.

Updates

#### It tells you, once, and then installs

DeepWork checks the public release list in the background on startup — never blocking the window, cached for six hours so it does not spend a rate limit, and reporting nothing back. A newer build shows up as a small pill beside the version, a system notification, and a card that offers Update when the release carries something it can run, or Download when it does not.
- Windows — the setup is downloaded with a progress bar and started; DeepWork closes behind it.
- macOS — the disk image is downloaded and opened for you.
- Linux — a.deb or.rpm goes to your installer, or an AppImage is made runnable and started.
- A release with only portable archives gets a Download button that goes to the file for this machine, and says why it is not an Update.
- Later is a twelve-hour snooze; Skip this version ends that release for good. A newer release is still a new question.

The tray menu

#### For the work, not just the window

The tray used to be a place to show or hide the app. It now carries the things you reach for in the middle of a session.
- New task opens quick-add from wherever the app is — expanding the widget first, because a 136×76 frame cannot hold a form.
- Settings brings the full window up on the right page.
- Pause offers 5, 10, 15 or 30 minutes, and Resume restarts only a timer the pause itself had stopped.
- The mute moved into a submenu of its own lengths: 30 minutes, an hour, four hours or the rest of today.
- Start with system and Always on top stay beside Exit, where they always were.

Taskbar

#### A pin reminder that tells the truth

Windows 11 keeps programmatic pinning for apps it has packaged itself. The reminder asks the shell first instead of pretending the request always works.
- The taskbar reminder asks the shell whether programmatic pinning is allowed before it offers anything.
- Where the request would be accepted, Yes raises Windows’ own confirmation.
- Where it would not — the usual unpackaged case — the button becomes Yes, show me and opens the installed-app list, where right-clicking DeepWork offers Pin to taskbar.
- The taskbar is re-read before every reminder and after every answer, so “already pinned” silences the feature instead of nagging through it.
- It is Windows-only and reports itself as unsupported elsewhere, because a reminder whose answer can never be observed should not exist.

Quiet & attention

### A pause that pauses everything

Pause, mute and focus used to live only in the system tray — which meant no way in on a Linux desktop without tray icons, in a browser tab, or on a phone. They are now one panel in four places, and each control means exactly one thing.
- Focus mode Hides the navigation and puts the timer on its own. Every reminder keeps running, because a focus session is exactly when the completion alert matters.
- Pause reminders 30 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours or until you resume. It stops the timer, the cards and the system notifications together, and restarts only a timer it stopped.
- Reminder sound 30 minutes, 1 hour or the rest of today. It mutes the tone only, so cards still arrive, and it expires by itself — even after a restart.

The same panel opens from the sidebar’s footer, the phone’s top bar, Settings and Ctrl+Shift+Q. The tray menu is one more caller, so Windows, macOS and Linux cannot disagree about what “Pause for 30 minutes” does.

The panel, shown on its own. Its three controls are independent: focus leaves the reminders running, a pause holds them, and a mute only stops the sound.

Answerable alerts

#### The clock can be driven from the notification

A finished session posts four answers with the alert: Pause, Next, Resume and Hold up. Next moves on and starts the next session, so answering is all it takes to carry on. The in-app card draws the same four, which keeps the alert answerable on platforms whose notifications cannot report a press.

##### Pause

Pauses whatever is running when it is pressed, even if the alert has been in the notification centre for a while.

##### Next

Moves to the next session and starts it, so one answer carries on rather than leaving a full clock behind a second press.

##### Resume

Starts the session that is waiting.

##### Hold up

Closes the alert and leaves the clock exactly as it was.
- The alert waits on screen instead of sliding away, and every button on it is an answer.
- Crossing it is not an answer: a swiped alert comes back after three minutes, and every three minutes after that.
- The startup, taskbar and water questions carry Yes and Not now on the notification too.
- On Windows, DeepWork asks the shell whether a notification is welcome — Focus Assist, a fullscreen game, presentation mode or a locked screen — and holds the suggestion cards. A session’s own completion alert still arrives.

Every screen

### Built for the device you are holding

Open DeepWork on a phone, a tablet, a laptop, a desktop monitor or a television browser and you get the same application and the same features. What changes is the layout: it is built around the width it is given, rather than shrunk until it fits.

The install dialog for a browser tab. The route is detected, not assumed.

#### It knows whether it is an app, a tab or a phone

The three surfaces have different powers, and the app reads which one it is instead of printing the same installation instructions to every browser.
- In a browser tab, one bar explains the one install route this browser actually has — Chromium’s address bar, Safari’s File menu, a phone’s Share sheet, or the honest “this browser cannot”.
- The system suggestion is offered once a week at most, and only when notifications are already permitted, so it never nags through a permission it cannot use.
- Installed, the app asks once whether to open with the computer and shows exactly where that setting lives on Windows, macOS and Linux — because a web app is not allowed to write a login item.
- Where the browser supports Document Picture-in-Picture, the installed app offers a small floating timer that stays above other windows.

Its own shape at every width

#### Seven layouts, one app

These are the widths at which the interface actually rearranges itself — the real breakpoints in the code, not round numbers picked to sound tidy.
- 1600px and wider — Room to spend. The dashboard widens the clock card and opens up its spacing.
- 1100px – 1600px — The desktop layout. The sidebar is a 240px column, and the wide two-column pages stay two columns.
- 900px – 1100px — One column at a time. A two-column chart page gives up its right-hand column before the navigation moves.
- 760px – 900px — The drawer. The sidebar slides away and a top bar with a menu button takes its place.
- 640px – 760px — One column. The board scrolls sideways rather than squeezing three columns into the width.
- 380px – 640px — The phone layout. Every multi-column grid stacks into one, controls grow to a thumb-sized target, and the fields stop iOS zooming the page in.
- 320px – 380px — The narrowest. Titles, subtitles and the calendar toolbar tighten to fit rather than overflow.

By touch

#### Fingers are not cursors

- Buttons, select fields, task cards and the drag grip all take a 44px minimum target.
- On a coarse pointer — a phone or tablet, including a touchscreen laptop — the scrollbars slim to 8px and stop reserving a desktop track.
- Text fields go to 16px below 640px, which is the size below which iOS Safari zooms the whole page in on focus.
- The outer padding follows `env(safe-area-inset-*)`, so the navigation and content clear the notch, the rounded corners and the home indicator.

By keyboard

#### And keys still work

- Escape closes the navigation drawer — and is what closes the topmost layer first.
- Task cards move along the board with 1, 2, 3 and the arrow keys.
- Nothing depends on hover, so no action is unreachable without a pointer.

#### No browser chrome

The web app is installable. Once it is on your home screen or your desktop it opens in its own window — its own icon, no address bar, no tab strip. It is the same application; it simply stops looking like a website.

#### The same app on the train

The browser build registers a service worker, so it keeps working after the first visit with no connection at all — on a phone, a tablet or a laptop that has gone offline.

#### It remembers how you left it

Your theme, your session lengths and your preferences are stored on the device and restored before the first paint, so the app does not flash the wrong background at you when it opens on a phone.

One thing that does not change: nothing syncs across these devices. Each browser and each installation keeps its own local database, so the same app on two screens is two separate sets of data — on purpose, and exactly as it is on the desktop. Moving work between them is a CSV export and import, which is written down in the FAQ.

How it works

### Four steps, and the first one takes ten seconds

#### Write it down

The round add button is on every page and Ctrl+N opens the same dialog. One title is enough — the deadline, priority and quadrant are already filled in with sensible answers.

#### Decide what matters

Drag it into a quadrant. That single gesture is what the day planner schedules from, and what Insights measures you against later.

#### Work in blocks

Start a session and the ring fills. The planner has already laid your queue onto focus blocks with breaks between them — so the next thing is decided before you sit down.

#### Read the week

Time by Task groups the sessions by the work they paid for, and Analytics turns the sessions, tasks, habits and entries into numbers and sentences — where the time went, which habits held, and what your best hours actually are.

Learn the method

### What a Pomodoro actually is

If you already work this way, skip ahead. If you have heard the word and never been told what it means, this is the whole idea in five steps — and then what DeepWork does with it.

#### The technique, in five steps

- 1 Choose one thingNot a project and not a list. One thing you could plausibly finish, or make real progress on, in a single sitting.
- 2 Set twenty-five minutesThe number is a starting point rather than a rule, and it is the one thing about the technique people most often change.
- 3 Work only on thatWhen something else arrives — a message, a thought, a job for later — write it down and go back to the one thing. The writing-down is what makes going back possible.
- 4 Stop when it ringsTake five minutes away from the screen. The break is part of the sitting, not a reward for it, and skipping it is how the third hour becomes worse than the first.
- 5 Every fourth one, stop for longerAfter four sessions, take a proper break — fifteen to thirty minutes. That is the shape of a morning, not a sprint.

The Pomodoro Technique is a method described by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s. DeepWork is an independent implementation of the idea — it is not affiliated with, endorsed by or licensed from the author of the technique.

#### How DeepWork implements it

The defaults are the classic ones, and every one of them is a setting rather than a constant:
- Focus session 25 minutes
- Short break 5 minutes
- Long break 15 minutes, after 4 sessions
- All four configurable in Settings

#### Why the size of the block matters more than the number

A block has to be short enough that starting it is not a decision, and long enough to get somewhere. Twenty-five minutes is a common starting point; what makes the method work is not the number but the three things around it — one task per block, a defined end, and a break you actually take. If twenty-five is wrong for the work in front of you, change it and keep the shape.

#### Plan the day in blocks, not in hours

An hour is not a unit of work; it is a unit of clock. A block is a unit of attention, which is why DeepWork plans with them. Decide what matters first, let the planner place it into focus blocks with breaks already reserved, and then look at the shape of the day you have made. When it does not fit, that is information rather than failure — Fit day will tell you how much longer the day would have to be.

DeepWork is what I build when nobody is paying me to, and it is the same argument in miniature: local-first by construction, reminders that wait for an answer instead of fading, and a page with no router, no animation library and no third-party script — because a claim that survives being checked is worth more than a stronger one that does not.

The honest comparison

### If you already use a Pomodoro timer

Not “better”. Different in the places that decide whether a focus app survives a real working day. “A typical Pomodoro app” is the common shape of the category, not one named product.

The comparison describes the common shape of the category, not a specific app — check the one you use. One more difference worth naming: DeepWork’s analysis is offline AI. It runs on your machine, over your own rows, and it never sends your day to a cloud model.

Questions

### The things people ask before they start

**Is DeepWork really free?**

Yes. There is no paid tier, no subscription and no account to create. The web app and the desktop installers are free to download and use.

**Where is my data kept?**

On your machine. The desktop app writes to a local SQLite database and the browser build keeps its data in your own browser storage. There is no DeepWork server and no sync. The desktop makes only the public GitHub release check, an installer download you press, and links you open; the hosted web app also counts visits, and that is the one exception — see “Does the web app count my visit?”.

**Does it work offline?**

The desktop app works entirely offline: its fonts, sounds and database are all local. The browser build registers a service worker, so it keeps working after the first visit and can be installed to your home screen or desktop.

**Do I need an account?**

No. There is nothing to sign up for and nothing to sign in to. Open the app and start working.

**Does it sync across my devices?**

No, and by design. Each installation keeps its own database, so nothing leaves the machine it was written on. A full JSON backup restores everything on another machine, and tasks can also be exported to CSV and imported back.

**Which platforms can I use it on?**

Windows, macOS and Linux as a desktop app, and any modern browser — including on a phone or tablet — as the web app. There is no native iOS or Android app.

**Can I use it for a team?**

Not currently. DeepWork is a single-person tool: it has no shared boards, no accounts and no collaboration features.

**What is Time by Task?**

A page that groups every focus session by the work’s title rather than by the task row. A daily Code review is a new task every morning, so counting rows would scatter the history; Time by Task shows one line with one all-time total, the sessions and active days, the first and last session, and whether the work repeats daily, weekly, monthly or is a one-off. It is at /time, and Ctrl+7 opens it.

**What is a standing reminder?**

A reminder for the things a normal reminder is worst at — a presentation, a class, a dose, a train — where you may be standing in front of a room and cannot answer. It is stored rather than scheduled, so closing the laptop does not cancel it; it escalates rather than repeating on a stopwatch; and it keeps asking until you press Done, Snooze 10 min or Stop. There is no close cross and no timeout.

**Will a standing reminder interrupt a presentation?**

No. It posts a sticky desktop notification and an in-app card, and it never brings the window forward. The notification carries the same three answers as the card, so the question can be dealt with where it is, without the app covering the thing it is reminding you about.

**What is the difference between pause, mute and focus mode?**

A pause stops the timer, the cards and the system notifications together, and restarts only a timer it stopped. A mute changes the sound only — cards still arrive — and expires by itself, even after a restart. Focus mode hides the navigation and leaves every reminder running, because a focus session is exactly when the completion alert matters.

**Does the web app count my visit?**

The hosted browser build counts visits with GoatCounter, so “is anybody using this?” has an answer without DeepWork running a server. It sends the page — path, title, referrer, screen width, language and time zone — never a task, a journal entry or an identifier, and GoatCounter stores no IP address for it. Count my visits is a switch in Settings, and with it off the script is never fetched. The desktop build is never counted.

**What happens if my database is damaged?**

A database that is present but unreadable stops startup with a card naming the file and the reason, instead of being replaced by an empty one that looks the same. Every launch also copies the database and its write-ahead log into a backups folder beside it before migrations run, and those copies are kept rather than rotated.

**Does DeepWork use AI?**

Yes — an offline one. DeepWork’s AI reads the sessions, tasks, habits and journal entries you already have, turns them into plain-language analysis, and shows you where your day is going, what is working and what to aim for next — so you can set a target and stay ahead of it. It runs on your own machine, from your own data: nothing is uploaded, there is no account and there is no cloud model to trust.

Something not answered here? Open an issue, email support@rajatmalik.dev for help with the app, or contact@rajatmalik.dev for anything else — questions are welcome, and the answers usually end up on this page.
